home.heroTitle: Cross-chain security across the software lifecycle
home.heroBody: The cross-chain Secure SDLC is a closed lifecycle of five phases; the three thesis studies secure the design phase, pre-deployment coding and auditing, and post-deployment operations and optimization.
home.sdlcBody: Each study is a self-contained module with its own page; there is no end-to-end pipeline coupling them.

chain.title: Real Solidity contracts
chain.body: Two in-memory EVM chains (py-evm): chain-A (id 31337) and chain-B (id 97). Every transaction is mined into its own block for easy observation.

ml.title: Compact algorithms, instant feedback
ml.body: ZKP, threshold signatures, CP-ABE and numpy/scikit-learn ML with fixed seeds — every action responds in under 3 seconds.

cd1.name: Π_univ
cd1.summary: Cross-chain academic credentials: the source chain anchors a Merkle commitment, the holder proves a business predicate in zero knowledge, a relay committee co-signs t-of-n and the destination chain verifies with ecrecover.
steps: Setup & key generation
Issue credential
Generate ZK proof
Cross-chain verification
Revocation

sw.title: Statement vs Witness
sw.statementHint: Relays and the destination chain only see this.
sw.witnessHint: Never leaves the holder's device; only used to build the proof.
sw.unsat: predicate not satisfied → proof will fail

tamper.title: Tampering lab
tamper.body: Each button re-runs verification under an attack; the chain-B contract itself rejects it via ecrecover, threshold and nonce.

shamir.title: Shamir (t, n) — nobody holds the whole key
shamir.body: Secret 1234 is split into 5 shares with a degree t−1 = 2 polynomial. Pick shares: with 3 shares Lagrange interpolation at x = 0 gives the secret; with 2 it fails.

charts.empty: Run the steps to see measurements

tour.s0: Reset the session: two fresh EVM chains — chain-A (university) and chain-B (employer).
tour.s1: Setup: deploy CredentialRegistry on chain-A and ThresholdVerifier with 5 relays and threshold t = 3 on chain-B.
tour.s2: The university issues 5 credentials: each is a commitment (hash + Pedersen); only the Merkle root is anchored on chain-A.
tour.s3: Student S3 proves “GPA ≥ 3.2” in zero knowledge — the statement is public, GPA and randomness stay on the device.
tour.s4: Relays independently check Merkle, revocation and ZKP, then sign; the gateway submits the fastest 3/5 → chain-B verifies with ecrecover and accepts.
tour.s5: The attestation record is CP-ABE encrypted: only ACME's HR or an Auditor can decrypt it.
tour.s6: Tamper: only 2 relays sign (below threshold) → the contract emits AttestationRejected.
tour.s7: Tamper: signatures from keys outside the committee → ecrecover yields unknown addresses, 0 valid signatures.
tour.s8: Replay an already accepted message → the transaction reverts “replay: already accepted”.
tour.s9: The university revokes S3's credential on chain-A.
tour.s10: S3 proves again: relays read the revocation on chain-A and refuse to sign → chain-B rejects.
tour.s11: Summary: the destination chain decides on cryptographic evidence, not on relay reputation.
tour.d0: Two simulated chains run inside the demo: chain-A is the university's system, chain-B is the employer that wants to check credentials.
tour.d1: Two real smart contracts are deployed. Threshold t = 3 means at least 3 of the 5 relays must agree before chain-B accepts anything.
tour.d2: Instead of publishing credentials, the university publishes a single "fingerprint" for the batch (the Merkle root). No personal data goes on-chain.
tour.d3: The employer only needs to know whether "GPA ≥ 3.2" is true. The ZKP lets it check that without seeing the real grades.
tour.d4: Each relay checks independently before signing. Chain-B does not take the relays' word: it recovers every signature itself (ecrecover) and counts 3 valid ones.
tour.d5: The confirmation is protected too: only people with the right role can read it; everyone else sees ciphertext.
tour.d6: The attacker controls only 2 relays — below the threshold of 3 — so the message is rejected on-chain. This is exactly the weakness behind Ronin and Harmony.
tour.d7: A signature from a key outside the committee is caught because the recovered address is not on the list — the kind of gap that cost Wormhole $326M.
tour.d8: Re-sending an already accepted message to get it accepted twice fails too: the contract remembers processed messages.
tour.d9: A credential can be revoked (e.g. after fraud is found). The revocation status lives on chain-A.
tour.d10: Relays read the revocation status before signing, so a revoked credential can no longer be confirmed.
tour.d11: The core idea: acceptance is decided by mathematics (proofs + enough signatures), not by trusting an intermediary.

primer.analogy: Like verifying a diploma through notaries: the university publishes only a "fingerprint" of the whole batch; the student proves they meet a condition (e.g. GPA ≥ 3.2) without handing over the transcript; a board of 5 independent notaries checks it, and the employer accepts only if at least 3 of them sign.
watchList: Issuing a batch of credentials and anchoring its Merkle root on chain-A
A zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) for a business condition
A 3-of-5 relay committee signs; chain-B checks the signatures itself
Seven kinds of forgery all rejected by the contract
termList: Merkle root|One hash that stands for a whole batch; changing any credential changes it.
ZKP (zero-knowledge proof)|Proves a statement is true ("GPA ≥ 3.2") without revealing the underlying data (the actual grades).
t-of-n threshold|At least t of n members must sign; losing fewer than t keys is not enough to forge.
Relay / committee|Independent parties that carry and confirm messages between the two chains.
ecrecover|On-chain function that recovers the signer's address from a signature — so the destination chain checks for itself instead of trusting anyone.
CP-ABE|Attribute-based encryption: only someone with the right role (e.g. ACME HR) can decrypt.

cd2.name: CrossGuard
cd2.topic: Vulnerability detection and auditing of cross-chain smart contracts
cd2.summary: Pre-deployment audit of bridge contracts: multi-source representation, few-shot classification, differentially private federated training and an audit report with protocol invariants.
steps: M1 · Multi-source representation
M2 · Few-shot detection core
M3 · DP-SGD federated training
M4 · Audit report
Exploit lab

desc.ex: Demonstrate impact on a real EVM

m3.note: 5 clients · softmax regression · DP-SGD (clip C, Gaussian noise) · moments-accountant ε · averaged over 4 seeds.

ex.pickVuln: Pick a vulnerable contract to run an attack.
ex.blocked: The fix blocks the attack — transaction reverted

tour.s0: Pick VulnBridgeNoNonce — a bridge that mints tokens on chain-B when it receives a relayer-signed message.
tour.s1: M1 builds the structure graph: release() mints but there is no processed[...] node — no replay protection.
tour.s2: M2 matches against class prototypes; 1-shot is confusable, 5-shot is clearer → “message verification error”.
tour.s3: M3: 5 parties train together without sharing code; DP-SGD clips gradients and adds noise, ε grows to 1.
tour.s4: M4 emits the audit report: high risk, invariant INV-NONCE as a candidate, plus a suggested fix.
tour.s5: Exploit lab: the attacker locks 100 on chain-A then replays release 3 times → receives 400 wDEMO.
tour.s6: The same attack on SafeBridge: replays revert with “replay: processed”.
tour.s7: The M4 report updates: INV-NONCE is now verified by the Exploit lab.
tour.d0: This contract accepts signed messages and mints tokens, but forgets to remember which messages were already processed — a very common bridge bug.
tour.d1: M1 turns the source into a graph of functions, variables and calls. The missing "mark as processed" step shows up as a missing node.
tour.d2: Real bridge bugs are rare, so the model must learn from a few examples. With more examples (5-shot) the distance to the right bug class becomes clearer.
tour.d3: Audit firms do not want to share client code. Federated learning lets them improve the model together while the data never leaves each party.
tour.d4: The result is more than a "buggy" label: the report gives the risk level, the violated safety condition and how to fix it.
tour.d5: Proof the bug is real: the attacker deposits once but withdraws four times by replaying the same message.
tour.d6: The fixed version remembers processed messages, so the second replay is rejected by the chain.
tour.d7: The invariant proposed by M4 is now confirmed by a real attack — a feedback loop between analysis and experiment.

primer.analogy: Like inspecting a building before handover: an engineer (M1) turns the blueprints into a structural diagram, an expert (M2) compares it with known defect patterns from only a few examples, several firms (M3) learn together without revealing their blueprints, and finally (M4) an inspection report lists the safety conditions that must always hold.
watchList: Bridge contract source code with bugs, and the fixed versions
Bug classification from very few examples (M2), private federated learning (M3)
Audit report + Exploit lab running real attacks on the EVM (M4)
termList: Smart contract|A program running on a blockchain; one small bug can lose all the assets it holds.
Few-shot|Learning to recognise a bug type from just 1–5 examples, because real bridge bugs are rare.
Federated learning|Several parties train one model without sending each other their source code.
Differential privacy (ε)|Controlled noise so nobody can reverse-engineer a party's data; smaller ε = more private.
Invariant|A condition that must always hold, e.g. "each message is processed once", "minted ≤ locked".
Replay|Re-sending an old valid message to get paid again.

cd3.topic: Anomaly detection and adaptive trust assessment in cross-chain communication

M2 · DS fusion & CRS
M3 · R0–R5 response & G-surv

kpi.invariant: Supply invariant violated: total minted on B exceeds total locked on A.

m2.noSeries: Run a few ticks to get r(t)

m3.noAuto: R4/R5 never self-execute — they run on-chain only after human approval.
m3.giniHint: 0 = even monitoring · high = concentrated on few actors

modal.title: Human approval required
modal.body: CrossSentry proposes a strong measure. Approving sends a real transaction to MintGateway on chain-B; reject if the evidence is weak (e.g. a validator that only co-signed by chance).
modal.whatR4: If approved, {target} is blocked on chain-B: every mint involving {target} will be rejected. Other actors and routes ({corridor} is the affected route) keep running normally.
modal.whatR5: If approved, the whole bridge pauses: no mint will be accepted anymore. This is the strongest measure, used when several actors misbehave together.

tour.s0: CrossSentry monitors a live bridge: LockVault on chain-A, MintGateway (7 validators, t = 3) on chain-B.
tour.s1: Normal traffic: every Locked is matched with its Minted, evidence leans to N, every actor's CRS stays low.
tour.s2: Switch to slow-burn: validator V7, with a good history, starts co-signing “inflated” mints on corridor A→B.
tour.s3: CRS of (V7, A→B) jumps while other corridors stay low → R4 isolate V7 is proposed; a human approves → blockActor on-chain.
tour.s4: From now on mints proposed by V7 are blocked (not enough valid signatures) — the traditional cumulative score has not even caught up.
tour.s5: Collusion scenario: V4–V6 co-sign mints with no matching lock; total minted exceeds total locked.
tour.s6: Several actors at R4 on one corridor → R5 pause bridge is proposed; approve → pause(), every later mint reverts.
tour.s7: G-surv: compare the optimal Θ with the concentration criterion off (w_g = 0) and on (w_g = 1) — balancing detection and fairness.
tour.d0: Picture a real bridge in operation: users lock funds on chain-A and receive them on chain-B. 7 validators co-sign, and each mint needs at least 3 signatures.
tour.d1: Every lock (top lane) is matched with its mint (bottom lane). When everything matches, the Explanation panel just says "matched" and everyone's risk stays low.
tour.d2: A subtle attack: a validator with a good history starts signing mints slightly larger than what was locked — small enough for a traditional score to ignore.
tour.d3: Risk is computed per (validator, route) pair, so only V7's cell on A→B turns red. The system proposes isolating V7 but does not act alone — the dialog asks a human to approve.
tour.d4: Once V7 is blocked on-chain, mints involving V7 no longer have enough valid signatures. The traditional score (grey line) still has not noticed.
tour.d5: Collusion: three validators and a relayer sign mints with no matching lock. Total minted exceeds total locked — counterfeit tokens are being created.
tour.d6: When several actors misbehave on one route, isolating them one by one is no longer safe. The system proposes pausing the bridge (R5); after approval every new mint is blocked.
tour.d7: Monitoring has a cost too: concentrating measures on a few people is unfair. G-surv (Gini) measures that concentration, and the response thresholds are tuned to balance detection, fairness and cost.

scHint.slow_burn: V7, with a good history, starts co-signing inflated mints on A→B.
scHint.collusion: V4–V6 + R3 mint without locks — the supply invariant breaks.
scHint.replay: R3 resubmits an already minted msgId (gateway in loose mode).
scHint.boosting: U5–U6 circulate tiny values to inflate reputation.
scHint.oracle_skew: Oracle O1 reports prices skewed +20–40 % on the oracle corridor.
scHint.flash_drain: U3 suddenly moves very large volumes — no rule fires, only the learning channel sees it.
scHint.liveness: V1, V2 offline — delays spread across all relayers: a systemic incident, nobody is blamed.

primer.analogy: Like a bank's security room: cameras at both doors (chain-A and chain-B) match every deposit with every withdrawal; two experts (hard rules and a machine-learning model) give their opinion, merged into one risk score per person per route; guards can warn immediately, but freezing an account or closing the doors (R4/R5) needs a supervisor's approval.
watchList: Two event lanes: locks on chain-A, mints on chain-B, matched pair by pair
The Explanation panel narrates every tick in plain words
CRS risk per actor–route versus the traditional score (M2)
R0–R5 responses and the human approval dialog (M3)
termList: Tick|One simulation beat; each tick brings a few new transactions on both chains.
Lock / Mint|Locking assets on the source chain / issuing the same amount on the destination; a mint without a lock signals an attack.
Validator / Relayer / Oracle|Party that signs / party that carries messages / party that supplies prices.
Dempster–Shafer|A way to merge two sources of evidence (rules + ML) and measure how much they conflict (K).
CRS|Risk score per actor per route; rises quickly on bad evidence and decays as behaviour returns to normal.
R0–R5|Response ladder: observe → alert → limit → extra confirmations → isolate actor → pause bridge.

nar.title: Tick-by-tick explanation
nar.empty: Press Run or Step — on every tick this panel explains in plain words what just happened on the two chains.
nar.pairs: {n} lock → mint transfers **matched correctly** (right amount, on time) — evidence points to normal.
nar.orphan: Chain-B minted {amount} tokens with **no matching lock** on chain-A. Signed by **{signers}**, relayer {relayer}. This breaks the supply invariant (minted ≤ locked).
nar.inflated: The minted amount is **{ratio}× the locked amount** (sender {user}, signed by **{signers}**) — the "value out > value in" rule fires.
nar.inflatedOracle: The minted amount is **{ratio}× the locked amount** on the oracle-priced route. Since the mint is driven by **{oracle}**'s price, the oracle takes the main blame, not the validators.
nar.duplicate: A message that **was already processed** is submitted again by relayer **{relayer}** — a replay attack to get paid twice.
nar.latency: Relayer **{relayer}** held a message for **{lat} ticks** before delivering it (over the limit) — a sign of deliberate delay.
nar.latencySys: {n} messages are late across **several different relayers** → recognised as a **system-wide outage** (e.g. validators offline); nobody is blamed individually.
nar.circular: **{user}** keeps sending small amounts back and forth with very few partners — suspected **reputation boosting** to be trusted later.
nar.learnOnly: No hard rule is broken, but the **machine-learning model** finds **{who}**'s transfer abnormal (p̂ = {p}) — e.g. unusual volume or frequency. Rules alone would miss this kind of attack.
nar.reverted: {n} mint(s) **blocked by the chain** ({reason}) — the approved measure is in effect.
nar.level: CRS risk of **{actor}** on route {corridor} = {r} → level **{level} · {levelName}**.
nar.proposal: CrossSentry **proposes {level} · {levelName}** for **{target}** (route {corridor}, r = {r}). Strong measures must wait for **human approval**.
nar.approved: A human **approved {level}** for {target} → transaction **{fn}** is sent to chain-B and takes effect immediately.
nar.rejected: A human **rejected {level}** for {target} — the evidence is not convincing yet; monitoring continues.
nar.paused: The bridge is **paused** — every further mint will be rejected until it is resumed.
nar.supply: Total minted ({m}) **exceeds** total locked ({l}): tokens on chain-B are no longer fully backed.
nar.quiet: No transfer completed in this tick — messages are still in flight.

world.title: Cross-chain Secure SDLC map
world.hint: Select a phase for details · double-click to open the study

p1.story: Before any code is written, the protocol must be designed so the destination chain trusts cryptographic evidence — not relays — without leaking user data.
threats: One party holding the whole key
contrib: Π_univ framework: public statement separated from secret witness
Predicate ZKP + t-of-n threshold signatures checked on-chain
Selective disclosure, revocation and CP-ABE access control

p2.story: Bridge contracts get a multi-source representation (structure, text, cross-chain operations) so a few-shot core recognises vulnerabilities from very few examples, and parties learn jointly without sharing code.
contrib: Multi-source representation: CPG + tokens + cross-chain operation types
Few-shot detection core (prototypes, attention fusion)
Privacy-preserving DP-SGD federated learning (FedVuln)

p3.story: Detections become an audit report: risk tier, evidence, typed invariants and fixes — then the impact is proven with real attacks on an EVM.
contrib: Audit report with invariants (declared / candidate / verified)
Exploit lab verifies invariants on buggy and fixed versions

p4.story: After deployment CrossSentry matches events across both chains, rates evidence competence (ECA), fuses it with Dempster–Shafer and tracks risk per actor–corridor pair.
contrib: Evidence with competence factors κ_L, κ_P (ECA)
Dempster–Shafer fusion with conflict K
Actor–corridor CRS with decay and jumps
R0–R5 responses with human approval

p5.story: Monitoring parameters are tuned periodically to balance detection, operating cost and how concentrated surveillance is (G-surv), so a small group is not over-policed.
contrib: G-surv: Gini index of monitoring intensity
Objective F(Θ) = w_d·U_det − w_g·G_surv − w_c·C_op

big.label: Big picture
big.title: The thesis in one frame
big.thesis: Cross-chain communication must be secured across the whole lifecycle: design on cryptographic evidence, audit contracts before deployment, and monitor adaptively after deployment.
big.problem: Cross-chain bridges hold very large amounts of assets and have suffered several attacks worth hundreds of millions of USD. Each lifecycle phase has its own kind of weakness, so no single technique is enough.
rq: How can a destination chain accept messages on cryptographic evidence while keeping data private?
How can bridge-contract vulnerabilities be detected when labelled data is scarce and code cannot be shared?
How can anomalies be detected and answered in a controlled, fair way while the bridge is running?
big.lifecycle: Life of a cross-chain message — threats & defending studies (hover a study to filter)

cd1.problem: Cross-chain verification often relies on relay reputation and leaks data when proving business predicates.
contrib: Three-layer Π_univ: arithmetic foundation → privacy logic → federated verification
ZKP (Groth16) predicates with statement/witness separation
t-of-n TSS committee verified on the destination chain, nonce against replay
CP-ABE attribute-based access control

cd2.problem: Bridge-contract vulnerabilities are diverse, labelled data is scarce and parties will not share source code.
contrib: CrossGuard M1–M4 pipeline for pre-deployment auditing
Multi-source representation + few-shot core (unitary encoder, Neural ODE, attention)
FedVuln: DP-SGD federated learning + RDP + DAA aggregation
Audit report with typed protocol invariants

cd3.problem: Operational attacks are gradual or coordinated; cumulative reputation reacts slowly and monitoring easily becomes biased.
contrib: CrossSentry: competence-aware evidence (ECA) from both chains
Dempster–Shafer fusion + actor–corridor CRS
R0–R5 responses, R4/R5 require human approval
G-surv: optimisation aware of surveillance concentration

inc.title: Notable cross-chain bridge incidents
inc.body: The largest bridge attacks of recent years. Pick an incident to see, step by step, what the attacker did — and, side by side, what would happen if the bridge were equipped with the thesis tools.

lesson.cd1: Several of the largest losses came from compromised validator/MPC keys or forged proofs: accepting on cryptographic evidence with a distributed threshold removes single points of failure.
lesson.cd2: Message-verification bugs, faulty initialisation and missing access control can be caught before deployment by invariant-driven auditing.
lesson.cd3: Abnormal outflows often ran for hours before anyone noticed: two-chain monitoring with approved responses shortens the damage window.

inc.source: Estimated losses, compiled from public post-mortems by the projects and security analysis firms.

poly.cause: A crafted cross-chain call replaced the "keeper" of the manager contract — the attacker granted itself withdrawal rights.
poly.defense: CĐ2: access-control invariant (INV-ACL) on admin functions; CĐ3: abnormal withdrawals flagged and paused with approval.

qubit.cause: Deposit logic bug: a zero token address was still credited, allowing unbacked mints.
qubit.defense: CĐ2: bridge-logic bug classified by M2, supply invariant (INV-SUPPLY) from M4.

wormhole.cause: Guardian signature verification was bypassed, allowing a forged mint message.
wormhole.defense: CĐ1: the destination chain itself checks t-of-n signatures with ecrecover; CĐ2: missing message verification detected.

ronin.cause: 5 of 9 validator keys were compromised (4 held by one entity), enough to sign withdrawals.
ronin.defense: CĐ1: distributed threshold committee, nobody holds the whole key; CĐ3: CRS + R5 pause when the supply invariant breaks.

harmony.cause: A 2-of-5 multisig; two leaked keys were enough to move assets.
harmony.defense: CĐ1: sound threshold + duplicate-signer rejection; CĐ3: colluding validators detected (Collusion scenario).

nomad.cause: A faulty initialisation made every message count as valid; hundreds of addresses copied the attack transaction.
nomad.defense: CĐ2: message-verification invariants (INV-NONCE/INV-DOMAIN); CĐ3: waves of mints without locks are flagged.

bnb.cause: A forged Merkle (IAVL) proof minted a large amount of new tokens.
bnb.defense: CĐ1: Merkle proof verification + binding commitments to the leaf; CĐ3: mints without matching locks detected.

multichain.cause: MPC keys were centralised with one party; assets were moved out abnormally.
multichain.defense: CĐ1: genuinely distributed TSS; CĐ3: sudden outflows trigger R4/R5.

orbit.cause: 7 of 10 multisig keys were compromised and the vault was drained.
orbit.defense: CĐ1: threshold and key distribution; CĐ3: abnormal withdrawal monitoring with approved pause.

player.title: How the attack unfolds
player.prevented: This step cannot happen — the attack was stopped at step {n} and the assets are still safe in the vault.

steps: The attackers send a fake job offer with a malware-laden PDF to an engineer at the operator. From the infected machine they obtain 4 of the 9 validator keys — all 4 held by the same organization.
5 of 9 signatures are needed to withdraw. The 5th comes from a partner organization that had let the operator "sign on its behalf" months earlier and never revoked it.
With 5 signatures, the attackers craft two formally valid withdrawal orders for the bridge contract.
The contract sees enough signatures and releases 173,600 ETH and 25.5M USDC from the vault to the attackers.
No monitoring raises an alarm. The breach is discovered only 6 days later, when a user cannot withdraw 5,000 ETH.
ronin.block: CĐ1: every signature must be bound to an independent committee member; delegated "sign on behalf" rights and keys of the same entity are not double-counted. The 5th signature is rejected — 4/9 misses the threshold, so the withdrawal is never valid.

outcome.real: ≈ $624M drained and detected 6 days late — the largest bridge hack on record.
outcome.with: The attackers still get 4 keys but miss the threshold; no withdrawal is accepted. CĐ3 would also raise an alarm the moment the vault drains abnormally.

steps: On Solana, the bridge's signature check reads its result from a "system account" supplied by the caller without checking it is the real one. The attacker supplies a fake account pre-filled with "signatures verified".
The bridge trusts the fake account and accepts a mint message never signed by the 19 guardians.
120,000 wETH is minted on Solana — with no matching ETH locked on Ethereum.
The attacker bridges about 93,750 ETH back to Ethereum, draining the bridge's collateral vault.
wormhole.block: CĐ1: the destination contract recovers every signature itself (ecrecover) and counts t-of-n committee members, never trusting a "verified" flag passed in from outside. No real signatures → the message is rejected and nothing is minted.

outcome.real: ≈ $326M; Solana tokens were unbacked until an investor replaced the 120,000 ETH.
outcome.with: The forged message is rejected on arrival. CĐ2 would also flag the "missing message verification" bug before deployment.

steps: A contract upgrade is initialized incorrectly: the value 0x00 is marked as a "trusted Merkle root". Since every unproven message has root 0x00 by default, every message now counts as valid.
The attacker writes a withdrawal message that was never sent from the source chain — the contract accepts it.
100 WBTC leaves the vault in the very first transaction.
The attack transaction is public: hundreds of addresses simply copy it, swap in their own recipient, and jointly empty the vault.
nomad.block: CĐ2: before the upgrade ships, M4 checks the message-verification invariant — "an unproven message is never processed". A trusted 0x00 root violates it, so the upgrade is stopped at the audit gate.

outcome.real: ≈ $190M drained by hundreds of addresses within hours — a "crowd heist".
outcome.with: The faulty upgrade never reaches the chain; there is nothing to exploit or copy.

steps: The cross-chain manager lets a message call any function by name. The attacker searches for a function name whose 4-byte identifier collides with the "change keeper" function — the one that decides who may sign withdrawals.
The message executes: the manager (which holds top privileges) calls the change-keeper function on itself and replaces the keeper key with the attacker's.
Now the "legitimate" keeper, the attacker signs withdrawals and the bridge accepts them.
Assets on three chains (Ethereum, BSC, Polygon) are drained to the attacker.
poly.block: CĐ2: the access-control invariant INV-ACL requires the change-keeper function to be called only through multisig governance, never from the arbitrary message path. M1 flags "arbitrary call into a privileged contract" — the hole is fixed before deployment.

outcome.real: ≈ $611M drained across three chains (most later returned by the attacker).
outcome.with: The change-keeper message is rejected for lacking privilege; the keeper stays, and no forged withdrawal is valid.

steps: The attacker calls the bridge's ETH deposit function without sending any coins. The ETH path uses an empty token address (0x0).
The "transfer token" call to the empty address does not fail — the contract believes it was paid and emits a successful deposit event.
The destination chain sees the deposit and mints qXETH for the attacker — completely unbacked.
The qXETH is posted as collateral to borrow and drain the protocol's real assets.
qubit.block: CĐ2: M2 classifies the bug as "bridge logic" and M4 derives the supply invariant INV-SUPPLY: minted tokens never exceed assets actually locked. A zero deposit does not increase the balance, so nothing is credited.

outcome.real: ≈ $80M borrowed out against collateral that did not exist.
outcome.with: The empty deposit is not credited, no qXETH is minted — the protocol is unaffected.

steps: The bridge uses a 2-of-5 multisig. The attackers obtain 2 keys — exactly the threshold.
With 2 signatures, they sign 11 transactions moving assets out of the bridge.
About $100M (ETH, USDC, WBTC…) is drained and quickly laundered through a mixer.
harmony.block: CĐ1: the committee threshold follows a safe ratio (e.g. 4/5) over independent members. The attackers still obtain 2 keys, but 2/5 is below the threshold, so no transaction can be signed.

outcome.with: Two leaked keys are not enough; the vault stays intact and keys can be rotated. CĐ3 can also detect collusion if signers behave abnormally.

steps: The attacker exploits a bug in the Merkle (IAVL tree) proof checker to build a fake proof for a packet that never existed.
The bridge contract checks the fake proof and deems it valid.
2 million new BNB are minted in two transactions — with no backing.
The attacker rushes over $100M to other chains before the network is halted.
bnb.block: CĐ1: the Merkle proof is fully re-verified and bound to the leaf content (leaf binding) and the chain context against the anchored root. A fake proof does not match the commitment → no mint.

outcome.real: ≈ $570M minted illegitimately; the whole network had to halt.
outcome.with: The fake proof is rejected; no new tokens. CĐ3 would also catch a "mint without matching lock" if one slipped through.

steps: All of the bridge's MPC key shares are controlled by a single person/infrastructure — "distributed" only on paper.
Once the key holder loses control, vault assets move out abnormally across several bridges at once.
The outflow is not stopped; the assets are unrecoverable and the project shuts down.
multichain.block: CĐ1: threshold key shares are assigned to independent members, each holding only one share. Compromising one party yields a single share — not enough to sign a transfer.

outcome.with: Losing one party does not lose the bridge: below threshold, assets stay safe. CĐ3 would trigger R4/R5 on an abnormal outflow.

steps: 7 of the 10 multisig keys are compromised — exactly the 7/10 threshold.
The attackers sign withdrawals that are valid as far as signatures go.
The first withdrawal moves part of the USDT out of the vault.
The following withdrawals take the USDC, ETH, WBTC and DAI — about $81M in total.
orbit.block: CĐ3: the first withdrawal is far outside the bridge's normal profile. Event detection + Dempster–Shafer fusion push the CRS risk score over the threshold → response R5 pauses the bridge (with approval) before the remaining withdrawals.

outcome.real: ≈ $81M drained in a series of withdrawals.
outcome.with: Only the first withdrawal gets through (≈ 15%); the bridge is paused and most assets are kept.

newbie.title: Four ideas to understand the thesis in one minute
cards: What is a cross-chain bridge?|Each blockchain is like a country with its own currency. A bridge is the exchange desk: it locks assets on chain A and issues (mints) the same amount on chain B. A group of validators/relayers confirms that the lock really happened.

Why are bridges attacked so often?|A bridge holds a huge vault, and chain B must trust what it is told about chain A. Steal enough signing keys, forge a proof or exploit one contract bug, and the vault can be emptied: the nine cases on the Real-world incidents page lost over $2.7B in total.

What is a Secure SDLC?|Building security into every phase of software — design, coding, testing/audit, operations, then feeding lessons back into design — instead of patching after an attack. Because it loops continuously, it is drawn as a closed ring.

What does the thesis contribute?|Three tools for three stages: CĐ1 designs a protocol verified by cryptographic proofs and threshold signatures (hard to forge); CĐ2 finds bridge contract bugs before deployment; CĐ3 monitors a running bridge and responds with human approval.

proto.title: Cross-chain communication mechanisms — how they work and how they fail
proto.body: The six main families of mechanisms that let two blockchains exchange assets and messages, following Buterin's (2016) classification and later surveys. Every simulation has two modes: the normal flow, and an incident or attack that happened in practice — so you can see exactly where each mechanism's trust assumption breaks.
proto.compare: Comparing the six mechanisms (click a row to simulate it)
proto.compareNote: The 1–5 scale is a qualitative, relative assessment; more dots = better on that criterion. Losses are the sum of the incidents listed above (estimates).

tri.title: The interoperability trilemma
tri.body: A protocol can hardly be trustless, extensible to new chains and able to carry arbitrary data all at once (A. Bhuptani, Connext, 2021). Positions are qualitative and illustrative.

proto.refs: References: V. Buterin, Chain Interoperability (R3, 2016) · A. Back et al., Enabling Blockchain Innovations with Pegged Sidechains (2014) · M. Herlihy, Atomic Cross-Chain Swaps (PODC 2018) · R. Han, H. Lin, J. Yu, On the Optionality and Fairness of Atomic Swaps (AFT 2019) · J. Harris, A. Zohar, Flood & Loot (AFT 2020) · A. Zamyatin et al., SoK: Communication Across Distributed Ledgers (FC 2021) · R. Belchior et al., A Survey on Blockchain Interoperability (ACM CSUR 2021) · T. Xie et al., zkBridge (ACM CCS 2022) · A. Augusto et al., SoK: Security and Privacy of Blockchain Interoperability (IEEE S&P 2024). Incident figures compiled from public reports by the projects and security firms.

notary.name: Notary scheme
notary.tag: A k-of-n committee watches and signs attestations
notary.idea: An intermediary — an exchange, a multisig group or an MPC/TSS committee — watches events on the source chain and signs attestations for the destination chain. The destination chain cannot check the source chain itself; it only checks whether the committee's signatures reach the k-of-n threshold.
notary.trustText: Trust an honest majority of the committee: as soon as k keys are stolen or collude, any message can be signed. The bridge is exactly as secure as k keys.
pros: Simple, fast, cheap; easy to deploy
Works with any chain and arbitrary messages
Easy to add new chains (the committee just watches one more)
cons: Centralization: a single point of failure in the key set
Key management and delegated signing go wrong easily (Ronin)
Low thresholds or many keys under one entity (Harmony 2-of-5, Multichain)
Opaque off-chain operation, hard to audit and monitor
normal: The user locks 10 tokens in the vault contract on chain A, which emits Locked(user, 10).
Five independent notaries watch chain A and all observe the Locked event.
Each notary signs the attestation “user locked 10 tokens”. At least k = 3 of n = 5 signatures are needed.
The bundle of signatures reaching the threshold is relayed to the mint contract on chain B.
Chain B only checks that the signatures belong to the committee and meet the threshold — then mints 10 wTokens to the user. Chain B never sees chain A itself.
attack: The attacker phishes an operator and steals 3 of the committee's 5 keys — exactly the threshold.
They write an order “unlock the entire vault to the attacker”. There is no matching burn on chain B.
The three stolen keys sign the forged order. Cryptographically these are 3/5 perfectly valid signatures.
The vault contract on chain A sees enough signatures and releases all assets to the attacker's wallet.
The two honest notaries cannot stop it and nothing raises an alarm. At Ronin (2022) the theft was noticed six days later.

thesis.cd1: Π_univ replaces “trust signatures” with “trust proofs”: the destination chain verifies a ZKP and a t-of-n threshold signature, rejects duplicate signers and keys held by one entity, and blocks replay with nonces.
thesis.cd3: CrossSentry matches events on both chains: an unlock with no matching burn is flagged immediately and R4/R5 pause the bridge with human approval — instead of six days later.

htlc.name: HTLC — atomic swap
htlc.tag: Hash lock + time lock, no intermediary
htlc.examplesLine: BTC↔LTC atomic swaps · Lightning Network · Interledger
htlc.idea: Both parties lock assets on two chains under the same hash lock H = h(s) and two deadlines T1 > T2. Whoever reveals the secret s can claim; after the deadline the original owner gets a refund. When Alice uses s to claim Bob's asset, s becomes public — and Bob uses that same s to claim Alice's asset.
htlc.trustText: No third party: only the hash function and both chains' time locks are trusted. But safety relies on synchrony: both parties must stay online and transactions must be included before the deadlines.
pros: No intermediary holds funds, no committee needed
Only needs a shared hash function and time locks
Atomicity: both transfers happen or both are refunded
cons: Swaps assets only; cannot carry arbitrary messages
Parties must stay online; congestion or censored transactions lose money
“Free option”: the first mover can walk away when the price moves
The same H on both chains links the two transactions (privacy leak)
Capital locked for long periods; needs a counterparty and liquidity
normal: Alice picks a secret s, computes H = SHA-256(s) and sends H to Bob off-chain. Only Alice knows s.
Alice locks 1 coin on chain A in HTLC_A: Bob can claim it by revealing s with h(s) = H; after T1 = 48 h it refunds to Alice.
Bob checks HTLC_A on chain A, then locks tokens on chain B in HTLC_B under the same H, for Alice, with deadline T2 = 24 h — shorter than T1.
Alice sends s to HTLC_B and claims the tokens on chain B. s is now public on chain B.
Bob reads s from chain B and uses it to open HTLC_A on chain A before T1, claiming Alice's coin.
The swap completes without anyone holding funds in custody. If Alice never reveals s, both simply wait for the deadlines and get refunded.
attack: Same setup: one hash lock H; HTLC_A (48 h) on chain A and HTLC_B (24 h) on chain B both hold the assets.
Alice waits until hour 23 — right before T2 — to reveal s and claim the tokens on chain B. She may have been watching the price (“free option”).
Bob goes offline, or his claim transaction is priced out / repeatedly replaced by a malicious counterparty (replacement cycling) and never gets included.
After hour 48, T1 expires. Alice calls refund on HTLC_A and takes her coin back.
Outcome: Alice keeps both the coin and the tokens, Bob loses everything. HTLC atomicity only holds if parties stay online and the network is not congested.

thesis.cd1: The same H appearing on two chains lets observers link both transactions. Π_univ proves conditions with ZKPs and selective disclosure instead of publishing a shared secret.
thesis.cd3: Monitoring both chains detects delayed transactions and blocking/replacement patterns near deadlines (CrossSentry's Delayed scenario).

sidechain.name: Sidechain & two-way peg
sidechain.tag: Peg assets to a side chain with its own consensus
sidechain.idea: Assets are locked on the main chain (peg-in) and an equal amount is issued on the sidechain — a chain with its own consensus, faster and cheaper. To withdraw (peg-out), tokens are burned on the sidechain and a federation/validators sign the unlock on the main chain; the sidechain may periodically checkpoint to the main chain.
sidechain.trustText: Security is not inherited from the main chain: you trust the federation holding the peg and the majority of sidechain validators — often only a handful to a few dozen nodes.
pros: Higher throughput, low fees, room for new features
No change needed on the main chain
cons: Few validators → much easier to capture a majority than on the main chain
The main chain cannot verify the sidechain's state
Slow peg-in/peg-out (confirmations, challenge periods)
Bugs in exit contracts/proofs (Polygon Plasma 2021)
normal: Peg-in: the user sends 1 coin to the peg address/contract on the main chain, where it is locked.
Wait for enough main-chain confirmations (Liquid waits 102 Bitcoin blocks) to avoid reorgs; the federation watches.
The federation (k-of-n) signs and the sidechain issues 1 pegged token to the user.
The user transacts on the sidechain: faster blocks and far lower fees than the main chain.
Peg-out: the user burns the token on the sidechain, the sidechain checkpoints to the main chain, the federation signs the unlock and the coin returns to the user.
attack: The main chain is protected by thousands of miners/validators — the sidechain and its peg rely on a small group (Ronin: 9 validators).
The attacker captures a majority of the sidechain validators/federation keys (Ronin 2022: 5 of 9 keys).
The captured majority signs a fake peg-out — no token was ever burned on the sidechain.
The peg contract on the main chain only checks federation signatures, so it unlocks and the vault is drained.
The main chain stays perfectly secure, but the peg does not: the main chain has no way to check the sidechain's real state.

thesis.cd1: A distributed threshold committee with independent members, plus proofs checked on the destination chain, means a peg-out cannot rest on “enough signatures” alone.
thesis.cd3: A peg-out with no matching burn on the sidechain is a textbook anomaly: CrossSentry matches events on both chains to flag it and pause with approval.

sidechain.lesson: main chain is safe — the peg is not

relay.name: Chain relay / light client
relay.tag: The destination verifies block headers and Merkle proofs itself
relay.examplesLine: BTC Relay · IBC (Cosmos) · Rainbow Bridge · zkBridge
relay.idea: The destination chain runs a light client of the source chain as a contract: relayers forward block headers, the contract verifies each header's consensus signatures (or proof of work) and stores state roots. To prove a transaction, the user submits a Merkle proof from the leaf to a stored root. zkBridge-style designs compress this verification into a single ZK proof.
relay.trustText: Almost no third-party trust: relayers only need to be live, not honest. Security equals the source chain's consensus — provided the verification code has no bugs.
pros: Trust-minimized: the destination verifies by itself
cons: Expensive on-chain header verification (different signature schemes and hashes)
Each chain pair needs its own light client → hard to extend
Depends on finality; reorg and long-range attack risks
Bugs in proof verification become the new trust anchor (BNB Bridge)
normal: Relayers keep forwarding chain A's block headers #100–#103 to the light-client contract on chain B.
The light client verifies chain A's validator signatures on each header and stores the state roots r100…r103.
The user's transaction sits in block #102. A Merkle proof π with the sibling hashes from the tx leaf up to the root is built.
π is submitted to chain B. The contract recomputes the root from π and compares it with the stored r102 — they match.
The bridge app on B executes (mints). Nobody has to trust the relayer; only chain A's consensus.
attack: The attacker builds a proof for a deposit that never happened on the source chain (a forged leaf).
The proof verifier (IAVL) is buggy: it does not strictly check the proof's structure, so the forged path still yields the stored root.
The destination accepts and mints 2 million unbacked BNB (BNB Bridge, Oct 2022, ≈ $570M).
Part of the funds leaves to other chains before validators coordinate to halt the entire chain — a very centralized remedy.
Lesson: trust-minimized does not mean bug-free — the proof-verification code is the new trust anchor and must be audited.

thesis.cd1: Π_univ binds commitments to leaves and verifies Merkle proofs together with chain/nonce context, so forged leaves or proofs used in the wrong context are rejected on-chain.
thesis.cd2: CrossGuard treats the verifier as a component to audit: missing message verification is detected and tagged with INV-DOMAIN/INV-NONCE invariants before deployment.

hub.name: Relay chain / hub (blockchain of blockchains)
hub.tag: Child chains share security through a relay chain
hub.idea: Instead of pairwise links, child chains (parachains/zones) connect to a central relay chain. In Polkadot, relay-chain validators check and finalize every parachain block (shared security); XCM messages travel between child chains trusting only the hub's consensus. Cosmos instead lets each zone keep its own security and connects them with IBC.
hub.trustText: Trust the relay chain's consensus — strong within the ecosystem. But shared security protects consensus, not each child chain's application logic; chains outside the ecosystem still need bridges.
pros: Cuts connections from N(N−1)/2 to N
Shared security and a uniform message format
cons: The hub concentrates systemic risk
Homogeneous only inside the ecosystem; Ethereum/Bitcoin still need bridges
A logic bug in one child chain can spread through the hub
Governance interventions (halting, burning assets) raise decentralization concerns
normal: Each child chain (parachain) submits its candidate block to the relay chain.
Relay-chain validators check and finalize blocks for every child chain — shared security.
Child chain 1 creates an XCM message sending 10 tokens to child chain 3; the message sits in a finalized block.
The message is routed through the relay chain to child chain 3.
Child chain 3 executes and credits the tokens. Both child chains only trust the relay chain's consensus.
attack: Ethereum, Bitcoin… are outside the shared-security perimeter: connecting to them still needs bridges — with all of their risks.
A misconfigured new liquidity pool on the Acala child chain (Aug 2022) erroneously minted about 3 billion unbacked aUSD.
Unbacked assets can follow XCM into other child chains — contagion through the hub.
On-chain governance pauses the child chain, freezes funds and votes to burn the erroneously minted aUSD — effective but highly centralized.
Lesson: shared security protects consensus, not application logic — code audits and runtime monitoring are still required.

thesis.cd2: Logic, configuration and access-control bugs in each child chain or app are CrossGuard's target: detected before deployment, with supply invariants (INV-SUPPLY).
thesis.cd3: Sudden mints without matching locks and assets spreading across routes are detected by CrossSentry; R4/R5 pause a route with human approval.

hub.spread: bad assets spread via the hub

optimistic.name: Optimistic bridge (fraud proofs)
optimistic.tag: Trust by default, allow challenges within a window
optimistic.examplesLine: Nomad · Across · Rainbow Bridge (NEAR→ETH) · rollup bridges
optimistic.idea: A bonded updater posts a message root to the destination chain. The message only takes effect after a challenge window (e.g. 30 minutes); during that time any watcher who sees a wrong root can submit a fraud proof to block it and slash the bond.
optimistic.trustText: A 1-of-N assumption: one honest, live and uncensored watcher is enough. The price is latency — and the assumption only holds if the contract is initialized and implemented correctly.
pros: Much weaker trust assumption than an honest majority
Cheap: no heavy on-chain signature/header checks
General and easy to extend to new chains
cons: Latency: wait out the challenge window (minutes → 7 days)
Watchers must be online, incentivized and uncensored
Cannot save you from implementation/initialization bugs (Nomad)
Griefing and attacks on the challenge mechanism itself
normal: The user sends message #42 on chain A; the bonded updater posts the root R containing it to chain B.
R is pending: the challenge window starts and the message is not executed yet.
Independent watchers recompute the root from chain A and compare it with R on chain B — it matches, nobody challenges.
The challenge window closes; R is confirmed.
Chain B executes the message (mint). Security needs only one honest watcher — at the cost of the challenge-window delay.
attack: A routine upgrade initializes the trusted root to 0x00. Every unproven message defaults to root 0x00 — so it counts as confirmed.
The attacker calls process() with a message never sent on chain A. The contract accepts it and transfers funds.
The attack transaction is easy to copy: hundreds of addresses just swap in their own recipient and resend — the vault is drained within hours (Nomad, Aug 2022, ≈ $190M).
Watchers are powerless: there is no fraudulent root to challenge — the contract code itself accepted everything.
Lesson: “one honest watcher” sits on top of “correct code”. Initialization bugs must be caught by auditing and monitoring.

thesis.cd2: Message-verification invariants (INV-NONCE/INV-DOMAIN) and initialization checks in CrossGuard's audit report catch “root 0x00 is always valid” bugs before deployment.
thesis.cd3: Mass process/mint calls with no matching lock on the source chain, and copy-cat transaction patterns, are flagged by CrossSentry and trigger an early pause.

ronin.name: Ronin Bridge
ronin.body: A 9-validator committee with threshold 5. The attacker took 4 keys held by one entity plus 1 never-revoked delegated key, draining 173,600 ETH and 25.5M USDC; noticed six days later.

wormhole.name: Wormhole
wormhole.body: 19 guardians attest (13/19 threshold). On Solana, signature verification read a caller-supplied system account without checking it, letting the attacker fake an attestation and mint 120,000 unbacked wETH.

harmony.name: Harmony Horizon
harmony.body: The Ethereum–Harmony bridge used a mere 2-of-5 multisig; two leaked keys were enough to move the funds.

multichain.name: Multichain
multichain.body: The MPC keys were in practice controlled by one person; after this person was detained, funds were abnormally moved out of several bridges.

orbit.name: Orbit Bridge
orbit.body: 7 of 10 multisig keys were compromised on New Year's Day 2024 and the Ethereum vault was drained.

freeOption.name: The free option
freeOption.body: Han, Lin and Yu (AFT 2019) show an atomic swap is equivalent to a premium-free American call option: the first mover can wait on the price and then complete or abandon, at the other side's expense.

floodLoot.name: Flood & Loot
floodLoot.body: Harris & Zohar (AFT 2020): the attacker opens many HTLCs and forces them to close at once to congest the chain; victims cannot claim before the deadlines and lose funds.

cycling.name: Replacement cycling
cycling.body: Disclosed Oct 2023 (CVE-2023-40231…40234) for the Lightning Network: a malicious counterparty keeps replacing the victim's HTLC-timeout transaction in the mempool until the time lock expires. Major implementations shipped mitigations; no exploitation was observed.

roninSide.name: Ronin (sidechain)
roninSide.body: Ronin is the Axie Infinity sidechain: Ethereum stayed secure, but the peg relied on 9 validators — capturing 5 was enough to drain ≈ $624M.

plasma.name: Polygon Plasma bridge
plasma.body: Oct 2021: a white-hat found that an exit proof could be reused to withdraw the same funds up to 223 times; ≈ $850M was at risk. It was patched in time and paid a $2M bounty.

bnb.name: BNB Bridge (BSC Token Hub)
bnb.body: An IAVL Merkle proof was forged because the verifier did not strictly check its structure; 2 million BNB were minted. BSC validators had to halt the chain to stop the outflow.

dragonberry.name: Dragonberry (IBC · ICS-23)
dragonberry.body: Oct 2022: an ICS-23 flaw let forged proofs be accepted by IBC, escalating to double-spends from ICS-20 escrow accounts. Patched in coordination across Cosmos chains; no funds lost.

poly.name: Poly Network
poly.body: A relay-chain design (Poly Chain) connecting heterogeneous chains through keepers. A crafted cross-chain call replaced the keeper key, enabling ≈ $611M to be withdrawn (later returned).

acala.name: Acala aUSD
acala.body: Aug 2022: a misconfigured iBTC/aUSD pool on the Acala parachain erroneously minted ≈ 3B aUSD; aUSD lost its peg, governance halted the chain and voted to burn the erroneous mint.

nomad.name: Nomad Bridge
nomad.body: An optimistic bridge: an upgrade initialized the trusted root to 0x00, so every message passed verification; hundreds of addresses copied the attack transaction.

rainbow.name: Rainbow Bridge (foiled)
rainbow.body: In May and Aug 2022 attackers submitted fake NEAR blocks to the optimistic light client on Ethereum. Automated watchdogs challenged them (in just 31 seconds in Aug 2022) and the attackers lost their deposits; no user funds were lost.

ctx.label: Research context
ctx.title: From the Internet of Blockchains to the research questions
cards: Internet of Blockchains|Hundreds of chains linked by bridges — each bridge a trust assumption and a pot of assets. See the map, the N² problem and a timeline of attacks.|Open the map
Interop protocol simulations|Notary, HTLC, sidechain, light client, relay chain, optimistic: watch how each mechanism runs and where it broke in real incidents.|See the simulations
Motivation & method|The argument chain, a risk-coverage simulation per module, the research gap and the closed-loop research cycle.|See the argument

iob.title: Internet of Blockchains — a network of blockchains
iob.body: Just as the Internet connects independent computer networks, the “Internet of Blockchains” is the vision of blockchains exchanging assets and messages with each other. Unlike the Internet, though, there is no common TCP/IP-like protocol: each pair of chains is linked by its own bridge with its own trust assumptions and code — and every bridge is a huge pot of assets sitting between two worlds.

graph.label: Illustrative map
graph.title: Chains and the bridges between them
graph.body: A small slice of the ecosystem (not to scale). Hover a chain to see its bridges; click a ! marker to see the incident attached to that bridge.
graph.cumulNote: Running total of the exploits on the map, in chronological order.
graph.hint: Hover (or tap) a chain to highlight its bridges.

stats: ≈ $|B|stolen in 13 cross-chain bridge hacks in just the first seven months of 2022.|Chainalysis, Aug 2022
|%|of all crypto stolen in the same period came from cross-chain bridges.|Chainalysis, Aug 2022
≈ $|B|lost in the 9 bridge attacks reconstructed step by step in this demo.|Real incidents page
| days|went by before anyone noticed the Ronin theft — no cross-chain monitoring.|Ronin incident reports, 2022

scale.label: Why the attack surface explodes
scale.title: The N² problem: pairwise links or a hub
scale.p: Illustrative yearly incident probability per bridge (p)
scale.riskHub: chance of ≥ 1 incident per year (excluding the hub's own risk)
scale.body: Each bridge is a separate trust assumption, key set, code base and asset vault. The number of bridges grows with the square of the number of chains, so even if each bridge has a small chance of failure, the chance that the ecosystem suffers at least one incident a year quickly approaches 100%. A hub cuts the number of links but concentrates risk in the hub.
scale.note: Illustrative model assuming independent bridges with equal probability p: P = 1 − (1 − p)^M where M is the number of bridges. Not a statistic.

layers.label: Layered model
layers.title: Which layers a cross-chain message passes through
layers.body: Like a network stack, cross-chain communication splits into five layers. A message goes down chain A's stack, across the transport layer, then up chain B's stack. Every layer has its own attacks — which is why defense is needed at every phase of the lifecycle. Pick a layer for details.

app.name: Application
app.ex: asset bridges · cross-chain DeFi · digital credentials
app.role: Business logic driven by cross-chain messages: lock/mint, burn/unlock, state updates, issuing credentials.
app.cd2: Detects contract vulnerabilities before deployment; audit reports with invariants (INV-SUPPLY, INV-ACL).
app.cd3: Monitors fund flows on both chains at runtime; R4/R5 pause with human approval.

msg.name: Message
msg.role: How a message is packaged: sender, destination chain, sequence number, content and any sensitive data attached.
msg.cd1: Public statements are separated from secret witnesses; nonces and chain context are bound into the proof.
msg.cd2: INV-NONCE/INV-DOMAIN invariants; the Exploit lab demonstrates cross-chain replay on the vulnerable version.

verify.name: Verification
verify.role: The mechanism that lets the destination chain believe an event really happened on the source chain.
verify.cd1: The destination verifies a ZKP and a t-of-n threshold signature via ecrecover; rejects duplicate signers and 7 kinds of forgery.
verify.cd2: Audits verification code: missing signature, source and proof checks.

transport.name: Transport
transport.role: Who carries messages and proofs from one chain to the other, when and in what order.
transport.cd3: Matches events on both chains; ECA + Dempster–Shafer and actor–route CRS detect delays and collusion.

consensus.name: Consensus & ledger
consensus.ex: chain A · chain B (PoW, PoS, BFT)
consensus.role: Finality and liveness of each chain — the foundation every layer above relies on.
consensus.cd3: Distinguishes system faults (lost validators) from attacks to avoid false blame; tunes monitoring parameters (G-surv).

time.label: Timeline
time.title: From atomic swaps to hundreds of chains — and the attacks
items: 2013|m|The atomic-swap idea|Tier Nolan describes swapping across two chains with hash locks and time locks — the precursor of HTLCs.
2014|m|Pegged sidechains|Back et al. (Blockstream) propose two-way pegs to move assets to side chains.
2015|m|Interledger Protocol|Thomas & Schwartz propose an Internet-style protocol for payments across ledgers.
2016|m|Classifying interop mechanisms|Buterin (R3): notaries, relays/sidechains, hash-locking. Same year: the Polkadot and Cosmos whitepapers, BTC Relay and the Lightning Network.
2018|m|Liquid Network|Bitcoin's federated sidechain launches; the peg is held by 15 members with an 11-of-15 threshold.
2019–2020|m|Hubs arrive, DeFi booms|Cosmos Hub (2019) and Polkadot (2020) go live; DeFi brings a wave of asset bridges.
2021|m|IBC & parachains|IBC goes live on the Cosmos Hub; Polkadot gets its first parachains. Assets locked in bridges reach tens of billions of USD.
08/2021|h|Poly Network|≈ $611M drained through a cross-chain call that replaced the keeper key.
2022|h|“The year of bridge hacks”|Wormhole, Ronin, Harmony, Nomad, BNB Bridge… Per Chainalysis, bridges account for ≈ 69% of crypto stolen in the first seven months.
2023|h|Multichain collapses|Centralized MPC keys; funds are abnormally moved out of several bridges. Same year: replacement-cycling attacks on HTLCs are disclosed.
2024|h|Orbit Bridge|7 of 10 multisig keys compromised on New Year's Day (≈ $81M). SoKs on interoperability security appear at top venues (IEEE S&P 2024).
2024–2026|m|Hundreds of L1/L2s, intents and chain abstraction|ZK light clients move from research to deployment; the number of cross-chain routes keeps growing.
Thesis|t|A closed-loop Secure SDLC for cross-chain communication|Proof-based design (CĐ1) · pre-deployment auditing (CĐ2) · adaptive monitoring and response (CĐ3), feeding back into design.

method.title: Why cross-chain communication needs a Secure SDLC framework
method.body: This page brings the thesis's arguments together: from the context and incident data, through root-cause analysis and the research gap, to the research cycle, the research questions and how each contribution is evaluated.
method.chainTitle: From context to thesis in five steps
chain: Context|The Internet of Blockchains is inevitable|Hundreds of L1/L2 chains coexist; assets and messages have to go through bridges.|/iob
Problem|Bridges are the largest attack surface|≈ 69% of crypto stolen in the first seven months of 2022 came from bridges; the 9 attacks in this demo lost ≈ $2.7B.|/incidents

Root cause|Vulnerabilities span the whole lifecycle|Trust assumptions and key management (design), verification and initialization bugs (code), late detection (operations) — no mechanism is immune.|/protocols
Gap|Solutions are fragmented by phase|Existing work usually targets one phase; there is no end-to-end framework with feedback between phases.|#gap
Thesis|A closed-loop Secure SDLC for cross-chain|CĐ1 proof-based design · CĐ2 pre-deployment auditing · CĐ3 adaptive monitoring, feeding back into design.|/

cover.label: Risk-coverage simulation
cover.title: Is a single module enough?
cover.body: Toggle each module to see how much of the real losses of the 9 attacks falls within its defensive scope. Each attack is tagged with the modules whose mechanisms can stop it (per the analysis on the Real incidents page).
cover.conclusion: No module covers everything on its own: root causes sit in different phases of the lifecycle. Only by combining all three — design, auditing, operations — do all attacks fall within defensive scope. This is the quantitative argument for a closed-loop Secure SDLC approach.
cover.note: Shares are weighted by estimated losses; “defended” means the module has a mechanism that stops or detects early the key step of the attack.

gap.label: Research gap
gap.title: Positioning against related work
gap.body: Representative works make strong contributions, but usually to one phase of the lifecycle. The thesis aims to cover every phase and link them through a feedback loop.
rows: SoKs / surveys|Zamyatin et al. FC 2021 · Belchior et al. CSUR 2021 · Augusto et al. S&P 2024|◐|◐|◐|◐|—|—
gap.note: ● main focus · ◐ discussed/partial · — outside the main scope. A qualitative assessment of each work's published focus, used for positioning — not a performance comparison.

cycle.label: Research method
cycle.title: A closed-loop research cycle
cycle.body: The thesis follows the spirit of Design Science Research (Peffers et al., 2007): identify the problem from practice, design and build the artefact, demonstrate it, evaluate it, and feed the results back into the design — mirroring the Secure SDLC feedback loop.
steps: Incident study|Review the literature (SoKs, surveys) and analyze the largest bridge attacks to extract root causes and bug classes.|Root-cause taxonomy; mapping incidents → phases → modules.|See the incidents
Threat modeling|Map threats onto the layers of cross-chain communication and the five Secure SDLC phases.|A layered model and a per-phase threat catalog.|See the layered model

Mechanism design|Propose a mechanism per phase: Π_univ (design), CrossGuard (coding – auditing), CrossSentry (operations – tuning).|Three frameworks/algorithms with explicit assumptions and guarantees.|Open CĐ1

Build & demonstrate|Implement with real Solidity contracts on two EVM chains, cryptography and machine learning; reconstruct attack scenarios.|This prototype: 3 modules, an exploit lab, attack scenarios.|Try the core playground
Empirical evaluation|Measure latency, proof size, F1/PR-AUC, FPR, detection time and monitoring concentration (Gini).|Quantitative results for each research question.|Open CĐ3

Feedback & improvement|Operational and audit results flow back into design: new invariants, new thresholds, new monitoring parameters.|A closed lifecycle — phase 5 feeds back into phase 1.|See the Secure SDLC loop

trace.label: Traceability
trace.title: Research question → method → metrics → demo
trace.cd1: ZKP (Groth16) for predicates with statement/witness separation; a t-of-n TSS committee verified on-chain; nonce-based replay protection; CP-ABE for access control.
trace.cd2: Multi-source representation (structure, tokens, cross-chain operations); a few-shot core; DP-SGD federated learning (FedVuln); audit reports with typed invariants.
trace.cd3: Two-chain event matching; ECA + Dempster–Shafer; actor–route CRS; R0–R5 responses with approval; G-surv and F(Θ) optimization.

limits.label: Scope & limitations of this demo
items: Two in-memory EVM chains (py-evm): no real network latency, congestion or reorgs.
Some cryptographic components (range ZKP, CP-ABE) are illustrative; the thesis figures come from the full implementations.
Incident figures are estimates compiled from public reports; the narratives are simplified for non-specialists.
The protocol scales and the positioning matrix are qualitative assessments meant to illustrate the argument.
